claims.text: Combinatorial deposition, such as LENS printing, can fabricate a single HfNbTaTiZr sample with a continuous composition gradient.
A compositionally graded HfNbTaTiZr sample will reveal systematic changes in mechanical properties as composition departs from equiatomic.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr forms a BCC solid solution.
The BCC solid solution in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is random.
Conventional arc melting or powder metallurgy produces the stated equiatomic BCC HfNbTaTiZr initial state.
Increasing the Hf percentage increases lattice distortion in HfNbTaTiZr.
Hf is a comparatively large atomic-size element whose concentration controls the degree of lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion impedes dislocation glide and thereby enhances solid-solution strengthening.
Increasing Hf above the equiatomic level initially increases hardness and yield strength up to an optimum concentration.
Increasing Hf beyond the optimum concentration causes embrittlement or a loss of ductility.
Variations in elemental percentages alter local defect structures that mediate dislocation motion.
Changing alloy composition can alter phase stability and cause an HEA to decompose into multiple phases.
A moderate range of Hf variation will retain a single BCC solid-solution phase.
Extreme compositional deviations may cause phase segregation or brittle intermetallic formation.
Rapid solidification and high temperature gradients are processing conditions typical of LENS.
The conventionally produced equiatomic alloy has documented mechanical properties suitable as a reference control.
Process-dependent kinetics during rapid solidification and interactions among the constituent elements may alter the quantitative response and optimum Hf concentration.
